column4: What support and resistance actually tell you
column5: Recognise prior reaction areas without treating them as promises.
column6: Look at each unmarked chart. Identify a broad area where price previously paused, slowed or turned. Then distinguish what the chart shows from what remains unknown.

column5: Describe broad structure before adding support/resistance zones.
column6: Choose a broad structure description for each chart before any zones appear. Use the visible swing sequence to support the label.

column5: Select consequential turns without marking every local fluctuation.
column6: Mark or name the swing points that most help explain the chart. You do not need to mark every wiggle.

column11: Compare against a reference set as one reasoned example, not the only acceptable answer. Invite the learner to remove one mark and explain whether the structure is still understandable.

column5: Choose defensible bands based on related reactions rather than a single exact price.
column6: Choose a band that captures the relevant reactions. Compare a too-narrow and too-broad version before making your own boundary choice.
column7: What reaction evidence anchors the band? | What supports the upper boundary? | What supports the lower boundary? | What relevant evidence would be excluded by a narrower band? | What unrelated movement would be included by a broader band?
column8: My first read was based on… | New evidence changed/did not change my read because… | I remain uncertain about…

column11: Keep chart scale and candle history constant while comparing options. Do not score pixel-perfect boundary matches; grade explanation and coverage.

column4: Choose the right areas and reduce clutter
column5: Keep the areas that explain the chart best and remove redundant marks.
column6: Review the overmarked chart. Sort candidate areas into keep, combine/reconsider, or remove. Then complete ChartLab study 1: Clear W.
column7: Which areas provide distinct information? | Which marks overlap or explain the same evidence? | Which marks would you remove, and why? | What useful context remains after simplifying?
column8: My first read was based on… | New evidence changed/did not change my read because… | I remain uncertain about…
column11: Preserve the learner’s initial choices until submission. ChartLab reveal follows submission. This is one of exactly three planned labs.

column5: Explain how wicks, bodies and closes contribute to a consistent zone boundary.
column6: For the selected reaction area, choose defensible upper and lower boundaries and explain which visible price features each boundary is meant to include.
column7: Which swings or reactions anchor this area? | Do your boundaries refer to wick extremes, bodies/closes, or a consistent combination? | Which evidence is intentionally outside the band? | What trade-off does your boundary choice create?
column8: My first read was based on… | New evidence changed/did not change my read because… | I remain uncertain about…

column11: Show guides and comparison examples only after the first attempt. Accept alternative boundary conventions when consistently reasoned and well supported.

column5: Simplify a chart without removing context needed to understand it.
column6: Start with the overmarked chart. Merge redundant areas, remove low-value marks and write down what you removed and why.
column7: Which two marks could be merged? | Which mark adds no distinct explanation? | What context must remain visible? | Does the simplified chart tell the story more clearly? Why?
column8: My first read was based on… | New evidence changed/did not change my read because… | I remain uncertain about…
column11: Show the clean reference only after the learner submits an edit and reasons. Do not introduce a ChartLab here.

column4: Evaluate a zone without inventing a magic score
column5: Judge contextual usefulness without treating touch count as a universal quality score.
column6: Compare the two candidate areas. Choose the area that is easier to interpret in context, or explain why neither is clearly preferable. Then complete ChartLab study 2: Uneven Lows.
column7: What do the interactions look like—not just how many are there? | Which responses, pauses or crossings are interpretable? | What wider structure affects your judgement? | What would make your conclusion less certain?
column8: My first read was based on… | New evidence changed/did not change my read because… | I remain uncertain about…
column11: Do not add a numerical zone grade. After submission, use the reference as explanatory guidance and discuss defensible alternatives.

column4: Read the approach to a zone
column5: Describe price behaviour before arrival and separate observation from interpretation.
column6: Compare a directional approach and an overlapping approach while the eventual interaction remains hidden. Later, study the instructor micro-case if its authentic source material has been supplied.
column7: How does the swing sequence progress? | How much candle overlap and back-and-forth movement is visible? | Is another meaningful area nearby? | What wider context is visible? | Name one thing the chart shows and one it does not yet show.
column8: My first read was based on… | New evidence changed/did not change my read because… | I remain uncertain about…
column11: Never replace the authentic instructor micro-case with a fabricated personal example. The controlled charts are practice only. Keep future candles, annotations and outcomes hidden in the initial case crop. AUTHENTIC INSTRUCTOR CASE REQUIRED; do not fabricate.

column5: Classify current evidence cautiously as rejection-consistent, possible acceptance, or inconclusive.
column6: At each reveal, describe the candle or sequence so far. Update the classification only when new candles arrive.
column7: What did price do within and around the band? | Where did the shown candle close? | What did the following candles add? | Is the evidence consistent with rejection, possible acceptance, or still inconclusive? | What remains unproven?
column8: My first read was based on… | New evidence changed/did not change my read because… | I remain uncertain about…

column11: A single wick or candle is not universal proof. Do not present fixed candle-count rules as universal. Let the learner revise the answer at each stage.

column5: Update a contextual assessment as the evidence accumulates or weakens.
column6: Move through the four timeline stages. At each stage, update the evidence log without looking ahead.
column7: What new evidence appeared? | What did not change? | How has your interpretation changed, if at all? | Is the area more useful, less useful, or still ambiguous—and why? | Are you relying too heavily on touch count?
column8: My first read was based on… | New evidence changed/did not change my read because… | I remain uncertain about…
column11: Do not rank a zone using touch count alone. The final state can reasonably remain uncertain if the sequence does not resolve cleanly.

column5: Distinguish a brief crossing from more sustained action beyond a zone.
column6: After the first crossing, record your current read. Then reveal the return or follow-through sequence and update the conclusion.
column7: What happened at the first crossing? | Did price return inside, continue beyond, or leave mixed evidence? | What additional evidence changed your read? | Would “not enough evidence yet” be more accurate?
column8: My first read was based on… | New evidence changed/did not change my read because… | I remain uncertain about…
column11: Do not reveal the end state in the initial view. The learner’s first view is about current evidence, not hindsight accuracy.

column5: Treat return tests and role reversal as possible developments, not requirements.
column6: After seeing a move beyond a former area, compare a return that holds with one that fails. State what would support or weaken each interpretation.
column7: What has price done relative to the former zone? | What evidence would make a holding retest more plausible? | What evidence would weaken that read? | What alternative remains possible? | Could no retest occur at all?
column8: My first read was based on… | New evidence changed/did not change my read because… | I remain uncertain about…
column11: Do not teach a retest as mandatory or role reversal as guaranteed. Show holding and failed return as alternatives.

column5: Read a failed break chronologically and preserve plausible alternative paths.
column6: Begin with the area before the attempted break. Record what you can know then; reveal the first move beyond and any return-through only afterward. Complete ChartLab study 3: Wider Neckline.
column7: What was visible before the attempted break? | What changed when price first moved beyond the area? | What later evidence challenged the initial interpretation? | How does the pullback-that-holds comparison differ? | What evidence would have been unavailable at the earlier stage?

column11: Never show the failed outcome in the pre-break state. Keep the alternate outcome visible in the debrief. This is the third and final planned ChartLab.

column5: Write conditional scenarios with evidence, alternatives, invalidation and available space.
column6: Use the unmarked chart first, then reveal the candidate areas. Write two conditional scenarios, or one scenario plus a justified stand-aside conclusion.
column7: If what observable event happens, then what interpretation becomes more plausible? | What is a credible alternative? | What evidence would weaken or invalidate the main scenario? | Where is the next opposing area, if identifiable? | Does available space appear meaningful, limited or unclear?

column11: This is analysis practice, not an entry signal or position-sizing calculator. Do not impose an unstated universal reward-to-risk threshold.

column4: Case study: a trade based on a reaction
column5: Review a genuine trade chronologically and distinguish decision process from outcome.
column6: Use the instructor’s genuine case only. Before each reveal, write your own reading of the current record. Compare it with the instructor’s contemporaneous rationale when evidence is available.
column7: What did the pre-entry chart show? | What zone and alternative thesis were actually recorded? | What was the stated trigger and invalidation? | How did risk and management unfold in chronological order? | What does the outcome tell you—and what does it not tell you—about process quality?

column4: When the thesis fails, or you stay out
column5: Separate thesis failure from process failure and review a genuine failed or avoided setup.
column6: Review an authentic losing/invalidated thesis or a genuine stand-aside decision. Record what was knowable at each stage before viewing the final outcome.
column7: What was the original thesis? | What evidence would have invalidated it? | What actually changed? | Was the process followed even if the outcome was poor? | If the instructor stayed out, what made waiting defensible?

column10: Case Study Review Sheet; instructor case required
column11: Do not turn a no-trade case into a fabricated loss or invent a failure narrative. Distinguish a sound process with an adverse outcome from an avoidable process error. AUTHENTIC INSTRUCTOR CASE REQUIRED; do not fabricate.

column4: Final chart review and knowledge check

column6: Work through the unseen chart in stages. Submit your full response before viewing reference analysis or the rubric details. Then complete the knowledge check.
column7: Describe the broad structure and supporting evidence. | Choose relevant zones and explain omissions. | Defend the upper and lower boundaries. | Separate observation, interpretation and uncertainty. | Write two conditional scenarios—or one and a justified stand-aside. | State invalidation and assess the next opposing area/space.
